object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account; everything hangs off it. Identified by account number, never reused even if the company returns.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: Six digit sequential identifier for an account, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product sold by the company, identified by product code. Fixed set today: CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.
Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that says what a customer pays and how often; generates the invoice line. Identified by plan code.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: Code identifying a price plan, e.g. CORE-MO-49.

source_references.excerpt: CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: The feature bundle a customer gets -- seats, API access, SSO, etc. Identified by its name (Starter, Professional, Enterprise).

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle

object_types.name: FeatureBundleName
object_types.definition: Unique name of a feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. ... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a certain amount on a certain cycle for a certain product. Identified by subscription ID.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: Unique generated identifier for a subscription, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription starts; mandatory.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription ends; optional, present only for fixed-term or cancelled subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The billing cycle of a subscription: monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The lifecycle status of a subscription.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

object_types.name: PausedFlag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean flag indicating a subscription is paused; not part of the status enumeration but overlaps with it.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, with its own identity, effective date, requester, and creation.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date... It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.

ambiguities.description: 'Plan' is used for at least three distinct concepts: the billing PricePlan (plan code, price/cycle), the FeatureBundle (feature set: Starter/Professional/Enterprise), and a sales-negotiated deal that 'frequently matches neither.' The sales-deal concept was explicitly deferred to another meeting and is NOT modeled here. Confirm whether the sales deal concept needs to be captured in this model or is genuinely out of scope.

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan. ... We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.

ambiguities.description: The relationship between an account and its 'active subscription per product' constraint refers only to ACTIVE subscriptions, but the modeled fact type 'Subscription is for Account with Product and PricePlan' does not distinguish active vs non-active subscriptions. As modeled, the external uniqueness constraint (Account, Product) should really only apply among subscriptions with status active/trialing/past due, not cancelled ones (an account could plausibly have a new active subscription for a product after a prior one for that product was cancelled). Need clarification on whether historical (cancelled) subscriptions for the same account+product are allowed to coexist.

source_references.excerpt: An account has one active subscription per account per product ... Can they have two active subscriptions to the same product? No. The system blocks it.

ambiguities.description: When an account closes and the same company returns, they get a brand new account number and are treated as a new customer for reporting, losing history. This suggests Account identification is per-registration rather than per real-world company, and there is no entity capturing the 'real company' across account closures/reopenings. Confirm whether a separate Company/Organization concept is needed, or whether losing this history is an accepted business rule.

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting. ... Which drives me mad, incidentally, because from a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history.

ambiguities.description: The PausedFlag is described as 'a separate boolean' that overlaps confusingly with SubscriptionStatus (a paused subscription may still show as active). It's unclear whether PausedFlag can be true regardless of status, or only when status is active, and whether there are any mandatory/exclusion rules governing it. No constraint could be confidently inferred beyond its existence.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: The commercial/business rule for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions (run-to-term vs prorated refund vs credit) is explicitly undecided and parked by the facilitator. The system behavior (end date set to paid-through date, no refund mechanism) is captured, but whether manual 'goodwill' credits should be modeled as a formal concept (e.g., a Refund or Credit entity) is unresolved.

source_references.excerpt: What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided. ... Put my name on wanting that resolved.

ambiguities.description: MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue) is explicitly derived from PricePlan price and BillingPeriod, and is not stored as an attribute anywhere in the source system; it was intentionally excluded from the object types/fact types per facilitator's decision. Confirm this exclusion is acceptable for the conceptual model, or whether a derived/computed value type should still be represented (e.g., for documentation purposes) despite not being stored.

source_references.excerpt: So it's derived from the price plan and the billing period. ... I'm not going to model it as an attribute of the subscription, then, because it isn't a fact anybody asserts -- it's a calculation over facts we already have.

ambiguities.description: There is a potential redundancy/consistency concern between the 'Subscription currently has PricePlan' (denormalised current plan field) and the derivation from PlanChange history: Priya states that if they disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is treated as a bug. This implies the current plan should ideally be a derived/view value rather than an independently stored fact, but it is explicitly stored today. Clarify whether the conceptual model should represent 'current plan' as derived (subset/equality constraint tied to latest PlanChange) rather than a separately asserted fact.

source_references.excerpt: So the subscription does carry a current price plan, and the change records are the history behind it. ... Correct. And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.
